Pathogen: Phytophthora palmivora fungus

Symptoms:
• Trunk & Branches: Pale chlorotic leaves, reddish-brown resinous exudate oozing from trunk wounds. Scraped bark reveals dark brown necrotic internal tissue; severe girdling kills the tree.
• Roots: Terminal branch wilting; feeder roots become brown, soft, and rotten.
• Leaves: Water-soaked light brown spots that rapidly turn dark brown or scalded-looking.

Prevention & Control:
1. Soil & Water Management: Improve drainage to avoid standing water. Balance soil pH to 6.0–6.5 with agricultural lime or dolomite.
2. Mechanical Method: Scrape away infected bark and apply fosetyl-aluminium 80% WP (80–100 g/1 L water) or metalaxyl 25% WP (50–60 g/1 L water) paste every 7 days until dry.
3. Chemical Control: Spray or drench with fosetyl-aluminium or metalaxyl at 30–50 g/20 L water. For severe cases, trunk-inject phosphonic acid 40% SL (20 ml/tree).
4. Biological Control: Broadcast compost-mixed Trichoderma around the canopy (3–5 kg/tree).

Pathogen: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides fungus

Symptoms:
• Leaves: Reddish-brown spots with well-defined margins expanding into concentric target-like rings across the blade, leading to desiccation and premature defoliation.
• Flowers & Fruit: Black floral rot and drop. Fruit develops small sunken brown spots along spines that rot upon ripening. Severe during hot, humid conditions.

Prevention & Control:
1. Canopy Pruning: Prune dense canopies to maximize airflow and sunlight penetration; remove and incinerate diseased branches.
2. Fungicide Spray: At onset of symptoms, spray prochloraz (20–30 ml/20 L), azoxystrobin (10–20 ml/20 L), or mancozeb (40–50 g/20 L) across canopy every 5–7 days.
3. Biological Control: Spray Trichoderma or Bacillus subtilis (BS).

Pathogen: Rhizoctonia solani fungus (prevalent in continuous rainy season)

Symptoms:
Initial scalded water-soaked spots changing to brown. Under high humidity, distinctive fine white mycelial webs bind leaves together in tangled clusters. Leaves wither and remain glued to twigs; severe cases lead to extensive shoot dieback.

Prevention & Control:
1. Pruning & Sanitation: Crucial to thin inner branches so sunlight reaches foliage. Rake and destroy fallen leaves outside orchard.
2. Nutrient Balance: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer during outbreaks to reduce overly lush new flushes.
3. Fungicide Application: Spray hexaconazole (20–30 ml/20 L) or copper oxychloride (30–50 g/20 L) every 7 days.
4. Biological Control: Apply Trichoderma 1–2 months prior to monsoon onset.

Pathogen: Phomopsis spp. fungi

Symptoms:
Small necrotic dark brown lesions surrounded by a prominent chlorotic yellow halo. Center of older lesions turns greyish-white with tiny black punctate pycnidia. The pathogen often remains latent until host trees experience physiological stress.

Prevention & Control:
1. Orchard Hygiene: Sweep up and destroy infected leaf litter to reduce inoculum.
2. Tree Nutrition: Ensure adequate water and balanced micronutrients to prevent plant stress.
3. Chemical Treatment: Spray systemic fungicides such as hexaconazole (20–30 ml/20 L) or difenoconazole (10–15 ml/20 L) rotated with mancozeb (40–50 g/20 L).

Pathogen: Cephaleuros virescens parasitic green alga

Symptoms:
Initially small, raised greenish-grey circular velvety spots. As thalli mature, they turn reddish-orange or rust-brown with a cushion-like texture on leaves and young twigs. Causes chlorosis, leaf drop, and twig dieback in humid, shaded orchards.

Prevention & Control:
1. Canopy Aeration: Prune dense inner branches to promote sunlight penetration and reduce microclimate humidity.
2. Foliar Spray: Apply copper oxychloride (30–50 g/20 L) or copper hydroxide (20–30 g/20 L) thoroughly over affected foliage with an agricultural surfactant every 7–10 days.

Characteristics:
Foliage exhibits uniform deep green color, smooth glossy cuticle, strong turgidity, and is free of necrotic spots, marginal scorching, or fungal/pest damage.

Management:
Maintain appropriate irrigation schedules and balanced macro/micronutrient fertilization matching vegetative growth stages. Continue periodic scouting to catch any early pest or disease signs.

Characteristics:
Anomalies not attributable to the 5 primary diseases. Examples include chewing insect damage, solar radiation scorching, micronutrient deficiencies (e.g. interveinal chlorosis), or mechanical/weather damage.

Management:
If symptoms diverge from the catalogued diseases, collect representative leaf specimens and consult local agricultural extension officers or certified agronomists for targeted diagnosis.
